title: The Mouse with Hats
content:
Professor Rocca was a plant scientist. He decided toprepare his farm before his two grandchildren, Apricot and Mandarin came in two weeks’ time. They were going to spend their summer vacation with him.

After the day passed, a weird rat appeared. He wandered around the house with a hat on his head. "How weird," Professor Rocca said. "I’ll get rid of him quick before my grandchildren arrive."

He got a fat cat with big whiskers to get rid of the mouse and get him out of the house.

The cat failed and the rat stayed. He appeared in the house every day. Professor Rocca didn’t know what to do. He was worried that the rat would get in his grand-daughters’ way.

His grandchildren finally arrived. When the saw him, they ran to hug him with their arms opened wide.

When it was late at night, Mandarin heard a voice under her bed. She shrunk from fear and said, "Apricot, can you see what it was? I really had a fright." When Apricot searched, they found the rat, but it quickly ran and escaped from their sight.

Tnhe ext morning, Professor Rocca got a trap and sad, "How about that?" "But you put nuts instead of cheese" said Mandarin. "It’s because that’s how mice are pleased" said Grandpa.

The rat smelled the nuts but before he ate, he thought, "it might be a trap" and quickly escaped.

He knew it was a trick so he put Professor Rocca’s socks on the edge of a stick and put it in the trap instead.

The next morning, he got his sock from the rat trap, and promised his grandchildren that he’ll take care of that.

Professor Rocca decided to start a plant war. He can’t bear this situation any more. He felt he should be a soldier in the field. For he can’t stay without socks any more.

Professor Rocca said, "Mice hate the smell of peppermint, and with these black pepper bombs, we’ll sure get rid of it." Apricot yelled, "We’ll get rid of him very soon."

The rat put on a protective mask, and stole Apricot’s sock.

Professor Rocca decided to use other plant weapons. He said, "I have a trick, it’s quick and effective." Mandarin said, "what are these strange plants?"

These plants are called "Venus flytraps. They mainly feed on flies, but they also feed eat mice, frogs and lizards. He can’t runaway this time."

A few days passed and the two grandchildren watched the plants. They found that they caught plenty of insects, but they didn’t catch the rat with the hats.

One night, they heard a scream for help. at that they were so happy and they said, "Finally we caught the hat rat."

When they went to see where the sound came from, they found that the tail of the fat cat’s tail was between the jaws of a venus flytrap.

While the hat rat was laughing at the fat cat Professor Rocca’s net came just like that.

THE END

title: Jimmy’s New Glasses
content:
It is a bright, sunny morning. Jimmy is up early. He is super excited about his first day at school.

Jimmy rushes to pack his bag. Then he dashes to get ready. His mom is making his favorite cheese sandwich for lunch.

In class, Jimmy sits all the way at the back. He squints and blinks, then rubs his eyes. “Why can’t I see the chalkboard properly?” he mumbles.

Jimmy moves to an empty desk in the front row. Mojo the Rabbit is sitting there alone. They begin talking and soon become friends.

Jimmy is curious about the object on Mojo’s face. “What is that thing on your face, Mojo?” he asks. “Oh, they are called glasses,” Mojo replies. “Glasses, wow! What do they do?” Jimmy asks. “Well, they help me see the world more clearly,” Mojo answers. “Does that make you look different from others?” asks Jimmy worriedly. “No, not at all. There is nothing wrong with wearing a pair of glasses,” says Mojo with a smile.

“Awesome! I think I might need glasses too,” Jimmy tells Mojo. Just then, their class teacher Miss Smith walks in. “Good morning, class,” she says. She turns around and begins writing on the chalkboard. “Please copy this in your books.”

Jimmy squints at the chalkboard. The letters seem too small and too blurry. “I cannot see the chalkboard clearly, but I am afraid to tell Miss Smith,” he whispers to Mojo. However, Mojo is eager to help Jimmy overcome his fear.

Mojo raises his hand and calls out, “Excuse me, Miss. Could you come here please?” Miss Smith stops writing and turns around. “Yes, Mojo. What happened?” she asks. “Jimmy wants to say something, but he is nervous,” says Mojo.

“What is wrong, Jimmy?” asks Miss Smith. “The writing on the chalkboard is too small for me to see,” says Jimmy nervously. “Aha, just that? Don’t worry, Jimmy. I will write a bit bigger for you,” says Miss Smith. “Never be afraid to ask for help. Nobody will growl at you or tease you,” she adds.

After school, Jimmy’s mom comes to pick him up. Jimmy tells her about not being able to see the chalkboard clearly. Miss Smith is listening too, and she nods her head. “I suggest you take Jimmy for an eye exam,” she says. Jimmy’s mom agrees. “Don’t worry, my boy. You will be all right,” she says to him.

The next morning, Jimmy and his mom visit the eye doctor. The doctor does some tests. She advises Jimmy to wear glasses so he can see clearly. He has a good time picking a pair of frames. Blue, yellow, or red? There are so many choices!

The following day, Jimmy goes to school with his new glasses. “Wow! You look even smarter in glasses,” says Mojo. “Thank you, Mojo. I got the idea from you though,” Jimmy replies. “The beautiful world seems much clearer now.” He laughs, giving Mojo a high five.

title: Ammachi’s Amazing Machines

title: The Garden in the Wardrobe
content:
Ma’s Jamdani wardrobe is a garden where hundreds of flowers grow and thousands of stars shine.

Ma shows me the saris and tells me about the patterns. “These patterns are woven out of cotton thread by the Jamdani weavers who live in a village by the river. There, water in the air makes the cotton soft. First they make the fine thread. Then, they sit at giant looms and use their hands and feet, one thread at a time, to weave a sari from the flower patterns that grow in their minds.'”“Ma, how do they remember all these flowers?” “Because it is impossible to forget something you love.”

Ma tells me what the patterns mean. “This one is a sandesh, a type of sweetmeat. And this one is a bitter gourd.” Ma points out the shapes woven onto the border of the sari.“EEEE! Why would you want bitter gourd on your sari, Ma?”“Because bitter things are good for you, my darling.”

“What is this pattern Ma?”“This one is special. It is called a chandrahar, a moon necklace. It is very precious because it took the light of many moons to make it. I wear it when I am happy with myself. This Jamdani reminds me that good things take time.”

My Ma says that many things will change as I grow up, but her love and the Jamdani garden will always stay the same. She says when I grow up, she will give me her Jamdani garden. This is my heritage, and I must keep it safe.

NoteThe Jamdani is one of the most complicated handwoven fabrics in the world. It is made completely by hand using only natural materials. A single sari can take weeks to finish, depending on the difficulty of the design, which is usually woven from memory. The designs are geometric forms inspired by nature. The loom is worked by two weavers, a master and an apprentice, who pass the needle back and forth as the master calls out the pattern instructions. This craft is recognized as an intangible heritage of Bangladesh.

Wonderful Wordsjamdani - a beautiful, traditional woven fabric made on a pit-loom powered by two weavers who pass the thread back and forth following patterns which the Master Weaver sings out.chandrahar - a pattern used in weaving. Jamdani weavers use this pattern to represent a necklace made of moons.

title: Commotion in the Palace
content:
The little princess was angry again."No, no! Not that one. Bring me the yellow shawl!" she shouted at the servant.

"This food isn't tasty! Bring me some fruit!" the little princess angrily commanded.

The little princess never spoke to her servants respectfully. She was never kind to them.

No matter how hard they worked, the little princess had no kind words to say. She always made them feel bad. The servants were very sad and very upset about the way the little princess spoke to them.

Her mother and father tried hard to teach her to be respectful to others. But she never listened.

One day her father told the queen, "I have a good idea on how to help the little princess understand the value of respect."

When the little princess woke up the next day no one was around. She shouted and shouted, but no one came. What should I do now, the little princess thought.

The little princess went to look for a dress on her own. “It took me so much time to pick a dress. My servants always helped me find a dress,” the little princess cried.

“It was too hard to clean my shoes,” the little princess thought as she walked out of her room. There were no servants around. She started to understand how much they helped her.

As she was walking on her own, she tripped and fell. The little princess started crying. Oh how I wish someone was around to help, she thought.

Her mother and father, who had been hiding and observing her all along, came to the little princess's side. "Mother, where are the servants?" the little princess asked.

"Well, we sent them home," the queen said, looking at the king. "I'll treat them kindly from now on. Please ask them to come back, father. They've helped me so much. Now I understand how I mistreated them. Please ask them to come back," the little princess said.

After that, there was no more commotion in the palace. The princess continued to practice talking to everyone respectfully and listening to them. The servants and the princess built love and respect for each other.

title: 3 Earth Tales
content:

One day in the forest, a fire began to burn. All the animals were forced to flee.

One small hummingbird stayed behind. It flew to the river, picked up a tiny drop of water in its beak, flew back, and poured that drop onto the fire.

Again and again, back and forth, it flew to the river, each time scooping up a single drop and pouring it onto the fire.

The other animals watched in disbelief from the far shore. They laughed and began to mock the hummingbird.

"Just what do you think you’re doing?" the animals finally asked.

Without stopping, the hummingbird answered calmly, "I’m doing what I can."

A man took a walk along a beach one day. He saw that thousands of starfish had washed ashore.

As he looked down the beach, he saw a figure moving like a dancer. As he got closer, he saw that it was a little girl, and she wasn’t dancing. Instead, she was reaching down, picking up starfish, and very gently tossing them back into the ocean. He called out, "Good morning! What are you doing?" The little girl paused, looked up, and replied, "Putting the starfish back into the ocean so they won’t die."

"Don’t bother, dear," the man said. "There are too many starfish. It won’t make a difference." The little girl listened politely. Then she bent down, picked up another starfish, and threw it into the sea, past the breaking waves. She then looked up at the man, smiled, and said, "Well, it made a difference for that one!"

One night, a King had a frightful dream. He dreamt that while riding his horse through the royal forest, the south wind called: "Beware of falling trees! Beware of falling trees!" Though the trees were beautiful and waved gently in the wind, the King was frightened. He turned his horse and galloped out of the forest.

The next morning, the King ordered his people to cut down all the trees in the kingdom. "We do not want the trees to fall down and hurt our children," he reasoned. "We will remove the forest and grow vegetables instead." The people liked the King’s idea, for now they had their pick of the finest wood in the forest to build houses and furniture, and the rest of the trees were sold at handsome prices to neighboring kingdoms.

Once all of the trees were cut down, the King felt happy, and relieved. But the people were unhappy. The trees had provided work for loggers and carpenters, and homes for birds. And while they missed their work, they missed the birds most of all.

Soon after the trees were gone, a dry south wind began to blow. It blew day after day. The vegetable crops began to wither and die. People huddled helplessly in their houses watching the wind uproot their gardens and scatter the dead plants across the land.

The King was worried. He called for his horse and rode through the fields to inspect the damage. There were no more trees to break the fury of the wind. As the wind blew faster, it swept withered plants and soil past the King, who watched dumbly as his kingdom blew northward. Lost in clouds of dust and drifting sand, fatigue overcame the King. Nodding asleep in the saddle, he heard the south wind call: "Beware of falling trees! Beware of falling trees!"

title: Chittu Makes Peace with Little Bear
content:
"We have to collect a lot of food today," Chittu said as she started collecting nectar with her friends.

"Oh no! What happened to our house?" Chittu and her friends exclaimed when they arrived back at their hive. They were in shock. Some bees were angry, and others were crying.

Some bees said, "It must have been the humans, so cruel." Others guessed, "No, this is the work of the monkey who jumps from branch to branch." Chittu wasn't sure, but she wanted to get to the bottom of it.

"We'll figure out who did this soon. But for now we have to rebuild the house and keep collecting food," Chittu said. Everyone knew it was the right thing to do. All of them started to work hard.

They built a beautiful new hive. But soon they saw someone trying to put their paw into the hive. Chittu and her friends acted quickly and chased away the intruder.

"Today we managed to save our house and food. But this isn't the end of it, I worry.” Chittu said. The bees were restless.

A few days later, someone tried to put their paw into the hive again, as Chittu predicted. It was a cub's paw. Chittu and her friends started to attack. Little Bear fell down with a thud.

"No, don’t attack him," Chittu shouted to her friends."How could you take the food that we make little by little by flying for hours?" Chittu asked angrily.

"My parents used to feed me but I can’t find them now. That’s why I came here," Little Bear explained, crying.

Chittu and her friends felt bad. They decided to give him honey every day. "But what will we do during the dry season when there aren't many flowers?" one of the friends asked.

Little Bear excitedly said, "I will keep the flowers in bloom always." and started working on it.

Little Bear filled the surrounding area with different varieties of seasonal flower plants. Soon the forest turned into a beautiful garden, and the bees and bear had plenty to eat!

title: Meeting Sasha the Mermaid
content:
The sun shines brightly, and the tide is low. The rock pools shimmer in the light. Mere is at her favorite pool visiting her friends. “Hello, everyone,” Mere sings out, peeking over the edge of the rocks into the pool.

Bluey the Fish is swimming in the pool. Crawly the Crab is sunbathing on the rocks. “Meet our new friend Sasha,” Jumpy the Prawn croaks.

Sasha the Mermaid emerges from the seaweed shyly. “Hello, Sasha. How did you come here?” Mere asks.

“Last night, a big wave swept me into the pool. But I was too weak to swim against the wave,” Sasha says. “You see, I only have half a tail,” she adds with a sigh. She swishes her tail up in the air.

“I don’t think you are weak,” says Crawly. “None of us could swim against a big wave. But anyway, what happened to your tail, Sasha?”“When I was small, I got caught in a fishing net. My tail got stuck in the net when I escaped. Now, some of the mermaids make fun of me,” Sasha replies.

“I know how you feel,” Mere says. “My right arm is weak, and some of the children make fun of me too.” She pats Sasha on the arm. “Let us be strong and not worry about what they say,” she adds.

“I need to go home, Jumpy,” says Sasha. “How can we help you, Sasha?” Jumpy asks. “Let us carry her out of the pool,” Bluey suggests.

“That would be difficult,” Mere replies. “I only have one strong arm.”

“Let us remove some rocks,” Crawly says.They push and shove, but the rocks are too heavy to move.

Mere has an idea, and she runs home. She brings back two floaters.

Mere gives the blue floater to Sasha. “I will use the red one,” she says. She helps Sasha wrap the floater around her body.

As the tide comes in, the pool fills up with water. Sasha and Mere float to the top of the pool. They swim to the edge as Bluey shouts out instructions. Jumpy, Crawly, and Mere hold Sasha’s floater steady. With their help, Sasha reaches the top of the rocks.

Sasha is thrilled. She can now swim back home. Taking a deep breath, she dives into the sea. She turns back to her friends and waves. “Thank you for helping me,” Sasha says happily. “Goodbye to you all.”

“Come back and visit us soon, Sasha,” Bluey yells. Mere and her friends wave back to Sasha. They watch her until she disappears into the sea. “I am glad we were able to help,” Mere says joyfully.

title: The Magic Horse
content:
THE TEACHING STORY The Magic Horse is one of the hundreds of stories collected by Idries Shah. In the Sufi tradition there is a continuum between the children’s story, the entertainment or folklore story, and the instructional or instrumental story. A story can help children deal with difficult situations and give them something to hold on to. It can, at the same time, stimulate a deeper understanding in adults. Through the instrumental function of this rich body of oral and written material, we and our children can now learn to develop the capacity to be more flexible and to understand many more things about ourselves and about life.

Once upon a time – not so very long ago – there was a land in which the people were very prosperous. They had made all kinds of discoveries in the growing of plants, in harvesting and preserving fruits, in making objects for sale to other countries, and in many other practical arts. Their ruler was unusually enlightened, and he encouraged new discoveries and activities because he knew they would help his people. He had two sons, Tambal and Hoshyar.

Hoshyar was expert in using strange devices.

Tambal was a dreamer who seemed interested only in things which were of little value in the eyes of the citizens.

From time to time the king, whose name was King Mumkin, would make this announcement: "Let all those who have interesting and useful devices present them to the palace for examination so that they may be rewarded."

Now there were two men of that country, an ironsmith

and a woodworker, who were great rivals in most things, and each delighted in making strange contraptions. When they heard this announcement one day, they agreed to compete for an award so that their relative merits could be decided once and for all, and recognized in public by the king.

The ironsmith worked day and night on a mighty engine with the help of many talented specialists. And he surrounded his workshop with high walls to keep his work secret.

The woodworker took his simple tools and went into a forest where, after long and solitary reflection, he prepared his own masterpiece. News of the rivalry spread, and people thought that the ironsmith would easily win, for his cunning works had been seen before, and while the woodworker’s products were admired, they were not very useful. When both were ready, the king received them in court.

The ironsmith produced an immense metallic fish which, he said, could swim in and under the water, carry freight over the land, burrow into the earth, and even fly slowly through the air. At first the court found it hard to believe that there could be such a wonder made by man, but when the ironsmith and his assistants demonstrated it, the king was overjoyed. He gave the ironsmith great honors, a special rank, and the title "Benefactor of the Community."

Prince Hoshyar was placed in charge of making more of the wondrous fishes and making them available to everyone. The people blessed the ironsmith and Hoshyar, as well as the kind and wise monarch whom they loved so much. In the excitement, the humble carpenter had been all but forgotten. Then one day someone said, "But what about the contest? Where is the entry of the woodworker? We all know him to be a clever man. Perhaps he has produced something useful." "How could anything be as useful as the wondrous fishes?" asked Hoshyar. And many of the people agreed with him. But one day the king was bored. He had grown tired of the fishes and the reports of their wonders which they so regularly performed. He said, "Call the woodcarver, for I would now like to see what he has made."

The simple woodcarver came into the throne-room, carrying a parcel wrapped in coarse cloth. As the whole court craned forward to see what he had, he took off the covering to reveal – a wooden horse. It was beautifully carved and decorated with colored paints, but the king snapped, "It’s a mere plaything!"

"But, Father," said Prince Tambal, "let us ask the man what it is for." "Very well," said the king. "What is it for?" "Your Majesty," stammered the woodcarver, "it is a magic horse. It does not look impressive, but it has its own inner senses. Unlike the fish, which has to be directed, this horse can interpret the desires of the rider and carry him wherever he needs to go." "Such a silly thing is fit only for Tambal," murmured the chief minister at the king’s elbow. "It cannot compare to the wondrous fish." The woodcarver was preparing sadly to depart when Tambal said, "Father, let me have the wooden horse." "All right," said the king, "give it to him. Take the woodcarver away and tie him to a tree so that he will realize that our time is valuable. Let him think about how rich the wondrous fish has made us, and perhaps when he has had time to think about how to really work, we shall let him go free to practice what he has learnt." The woodcarver was taken away, and Prince Tambal left the court carrying the magic horse.

Tambal took the horse to his rooms, and he discovered that it had several knobs, cleverly concealed in the carved designs. When these were turned in a certain manner, the horse – and anyone mounted on it – rose into the air and sped to whatever place was in the mind of the person who moved the knobs.

In this way, day after day, Tambal flew to places he had never visited before, and he came to know a great many things. He took the horse with him everywhere.

One day he met Hoshyar, who said to him, "Carrying a wooden horse is just the thing for someone like you. As for me, I am working for the good of all, towards my heart’s desire!" Tambal thought, "I wish I knew what the good of all is. And I wish I could know what my heart’s desire is." When he was next in his room, he sat upon the horse, turned the knobs, and thought, "I would like to find my heart’s desire." More swiftly than light, the horse rose into the air and carried the prince a thousand ordinary days away to a far kingdom that was ruled by a magician-king.

The king, whose name was Kahana, had a beautiful daughter called Precious Pearl.

In order to protect her, he had imprisoned her in a palace that wheeled in the sky, higher than any mortal could reach. As Tambal was approaching the magic land, he saw the glittering palace in the heavens, and he alighted there. The princess and the young horseman met and fell in love. "My father will never allow us to marry," she said, "for he has commanded that I must marry the son of another magician-king who lives across the cold desert to the east of our homeland. He wants to unify the two kingdoms by this marriage, and no one dares to disobey him." "I will go to him and try to reason with him," said Tambal, mounting the magic horse. But when he descended into the magic land, there were so many new and exciting things to see that he did not hurry to the palace. When he finally arrived, the drum at the gate was beating, which meant that the king was absent. Tambal asked when the king would return. "He has gone to visit his daughter in the Whirling Palace," said a man on the street, "and he usually spends several hours with her."

Tambal went to a quiet place where he willed the horse to carry him to the king’s private apartment. "I will approach him in his own home," he thought to himself, "for if I go to the Whirling Palace without his permission, he may be angry." When he got to the king’s apartment, he hid behind some curtains and lay down to sleep.

Meanwhile, unable to keep her secret, Princess Precious Pearl had confessed to her father that a man on a flying horse had visited her and wanted to marry her. King Kahana was furious. He placed sentries around the Whirling Palace and returned to his own apartment to think things over. As soon as he entered his bedchamber, one of his tongueless magic servants guarding it pointed to the wooden horse lying in a corner. "Aha!" exclaimed the magician-king. "Now I have him. Let us look at this horse and see what manner of thing it may be." As he and his servants were examining the horse, the prince slipped away and hid in another part of the palace. The king twisted the knobs, tapped the horse, and tried to understand how it worked, but he was baffled. "Take that thing away," he said. "It has no use now, if it ever had any. It is just a toy, fit only for children."

And so the horse was put into a cupboard. Now King Kahana thought that he should arrange his daughter’s wedding without delay in case the man with the horse had other ways to win her. So he called her to his palace and sent a message to the other magician-king, whose son was to marry Princess Precious Pearl, asking that the prince be sent to claim his bride. Meanwhile, Prince Tambal escaped from the palace when the guards were asleep and decided to return to his own country. His quest for his heart’s desire now seemed almost hopeless, but he said to himself, "If it takes the rest of my life, I shall return with troops to take this kingdom by force. I can do that only by convincing my father that I must have his help to attain my heart’s desire."

So saying, he set off. Never was a man worse equipped for such a journey. An alien, traveling on foot, without any kind of provisions, facing pitiless heat, freezing nights, and sandstorms, he soon became hopelessly lost in the desert.

Delirious, Tambal blamed himself, his father, the magician-king, the woodcarver, even the princess and the magic horse itself. Sometimes he thought he saw water ahead of him, sometimes fair cities. Sometimes he felt elated, sometimes incomparably sad. Sometimes he thought he had companions in his difficulties, but when he shook himself he saw that he was quite alone.

He felt that he had been traveling for an eternity. Suddenly, when he had given up and started again several times, he saw something right in front of him that at first looked like a mirage. It was a garden full of delicious fruits that sparkled and beckoned him to come closer. At first Tambal did not take much notice and continued walking, but soon he realized that he was passing through such a garden. He gathered some of the fruits and tasted them cautiously. They were delicious. They took away his fear as well as his hunger and thirst. When he was full, he lay down in the shade of a huge, welcoming tree and fell asleep.

When he woke up he felt well enough, but something seemed to be wrong. Running to a nearby pool, he looked at his reflection in the water. Staring up at him was a horrible sight. He saw a long beard, curved horns, and ears a foot long. He looked down at his hands. They were covered with fur. Was it a nightmare? Pinching and beating himself, he tried to wake up. But it was no use. Beside himself with fear and horror, screaming and sobbing, he threw himself on the ground. "Whether I live or die," he thought, "these fruits have ruined me. Even with the greatest army of all time, conquest will not help me. Nobody would marry me now, especially not Princess Precious Pearl. Even beasts would be terrified at the sight of me, and my heart’s desire would surely reject me!" And he lost consciousness.

When he woke again, in the dark, he saw a light approaching through the groves of silent trees. Fear and hope struggled in him. As the light came closer, he saw that it was a lamp enclosed in a brilliant starlike shape. The lamp was carried by a bearded man who walked in the pool of brightness that it cast around. "My son," said the man to Tambal, "you have been affected by the influences of this place. If I had not come along, you would have remained just another beast of this enchanted grove, for there are many more like you. But I can help you." Tambal wondered whether this man was a fiend in disguise, perhaps the very owner of the evil trees. But, as his sense returned, he realized that he had nothing to lose. "Help me, Father," he said. "If you really want your heart’s desire," said the wise man, "you have only to fix this desire firmly in your mind, not thinking of the fresh, delicious fruit. You must then take up some of the dried fruits that are lying at the foot of all these trees and eat them. Then follow your destiny." So saying, he walked away. As the sage’s light disappeared into the darkness, Tambal saw that the moon was rising, and in its pale light he could see that there were indeed piles of dried fruits under every tree. He gathered some and ate them as quickly as he could. Slowly the fur disappeared from his hands and arms. The horns shrank, then vanished. The beard fell away. He was himself again.

By now it was first light, and in the dawn he heard the tinkling of camel bells. A grand procession was coming through the enchanted forest. As Tambal stood there, two riders pulled away from the glittering line of people and animals and galloped up to him. "In the name of the prince, our lord, we demand some of your fruit. His celestial highness is thirsty and has a desire for some of these strange apricots," said an officer. Tambal did not move, still numb from his recent experiences. Now the prince himself came down from his carriage and said, "I am Jadugarzada, son of the magician-king of the East. Here is a bag of gold, oaf. I am having some of your fruit, because I am desirous of it. I am in a hurry to claim my bride, Princess Precious Pearl, daughter of Kahana, magician-king of the West." At these words Tambal’s heart turned over. But realizing that this must be the destiny which the sage had told him to follow, he offered the prince as much of the fruit as he could eat. When the prince had eaten, he began to fall asleep. As he did so, horns, fur and huge ears started to grow out of him. When the soldiers shook him, the prince began to behave in a strange way. He claimed that he was normal, and that they were deformed. The prince’s councilors restrained him and held a hurried debate. Tambal claimed that all would have been well if the prince had not fallen asleep. Finally it was decided to put Tambal in the carriage and have him play the part of the prince. The horned Jadugarzada was tied to a horse with a veil thrown over his face, disguised as a servant woman. "He may recover his wits eventually," said the councilors, "and, in any case, he is still our prince. Tambal shall marry the girl. Then, as soon as possible, we shall carry them all back to our own country for our king to solve the problem." Tambal, biding his time and following his destiny, agreed to his own part in the masquerade.

When the party arrived at the capital of the West, the king himself came out to meet them, and Tambal was taken to the princess as her bridegroom. She was so astonished that she nearly fainted, but Tambal whispered quickly what had happened. And so they were married, and the people had a great celebration. In the meantime the horned prince had half recovered his wits, but not his human form, and his escort still kept him under cover. As soon as the feasting was over, the chief of the horned prince’s party (who had been keeping Tambal and the princess under a very close watch) presented himself to the court. He said, "O Just and Glorious Monarch, Fountain of Wisdom, the time has now come, according to the pronouncements of our astrologers and soothsayers, to conduct the bridal pair back to our own land, so that they may be established in their new home under the most felicitous circumstances and influences." The princess turned to Tambal in alarm, for she knew that as soon as they were on the open road, Jadugarzada would claim her and make an end of Tambal.

Tambal whispered to her, "Fear nothing. We must act as best we can, following our destiny. Agree to go, but say that you will not travel without the wooden horse." At first the magician-king was annoyed at this wish of his daughter’s. He realized that she wanted the horse because it was connected with her first suitor. But the chief minister of the horned prince said, "Majesty, this is just the desire for a toy, such as any young girl might have. Let her have her plaything so that we may make haste homeward."

So the magician-king agreed, and soon the splendid procession was on its way. After the king’s escort had withdrawn, and before the party stopped for the night, the hideous Jadugarzada threw off his veil and cried out to Tambal, "Miserable author of my misfortunes! I will bind you hand and foot and take you back to my own land. Then you must tell me how to remove this enchantment, or I will have you flayed alive, inch by inch. Now, give me the Princess Precious Pearl!"

Tambal ran to the princess and, in front of the astonished party, rose into the sky on the wooden horse with Precious Pearl mounted behind him. In minutes the couple alighted at the palace of King Mumkin. They related everything that had happened to them, and the king was almost overcome with delight at their safe return. He at once gave orders for the woodcarver to be released, rewarded, and applauded by all the citizens.

When King Mumkin was gathered to his fathers, Princess Precious Pearl and Prince Tambal succeeded him. Prince Hoshyar was pleased, too, because he was still entranced by the wondrous fish. "I am glad for your own sakes, if you are happy," he said to them, "but I think there is nothing more rewarding than my work with the wondrous fish."

And this story is the origin of a strange saying among the people of that land, although they have forgotten its beginnings. The saying is: "Those who want fish can achieve much through fish, and those who do not know their heart’s desire may first have to hear the story of the wooden horse."

title: Panam City
content:
"Mira, do you know there is a ghost capital in Bangladesh?" asked Nahian."Don't be silly, Dhaka is the capital of Bangladesh," replied Mira."Today it is. But it was not always this way. In the 15 00 's, Bengal was divided into many independent states. Panam City was the capital of the kingdom of courageous Isa Khan, one of the last of the Baro-Bhuyan landlords. But after Isa Khan died, the Mughals took over the land.”

“Is it the ghost of Isa Khan that haunts Panam City?” asked Mira."He, among many others! The city had many rulers. After the Mughals, the British East India Company took over and set up their textile offices here.”“So, Dhaka has a long history of textiles!” Mira was shocked to learn that the textile trade has so much history. “Oh yes, Bengal was famous for a fine fabric called muslin. It was so thin that a six-yard sari could be folded and passed through a finger ring. Panam Nagar was home to the best muslin weavers and many merchants moved here and built fantastic mansions. At the peak of its glory, the city had close to 14 00 families.”

“Oh wow, it must have been a great place to live back then!” Mira imagined the bustling city."It was. There were grand balls, festivals, and celebrations. But if you visit Panam City today, it is quiet and still. You will find only one street that is lined with 52 broken mansions. These houses were once grand palaces, but today they are empty and falling apart. Only dogs and trees live in Panam today. "

“Oh wow! What happened? Did the ghosts drive everybody out?” Mira loved a good scary story. "Some say that there was a fire. Others say that when the British Raj fell apart, the people of the area started fighting. For hundreds of years, the Hindus and Muslims had lived together, but they stopped sharing the land, things fell apart, and people moved out. This is why today many people call it the Ghost City.”

“Oh dear, that sounds sad more than scary," said Mira. "It's true. But visiting Panam feels like time travel. In Dhaka everything is new, and the buildings are tall. But in Panam Nagar, everything feels frozen in time,” replied Nahian.

NotePanam Nagar was the capital city of medieval Bengal. Close to the Meghna River in Sonargaon, it was once a very wealthy city. Today only a small part of it remains. The street of 52 houses is an open-air museum protected as a Heritage Site by the Bangladesh Government.

title: Friends from Another World
content:
My name is Onno. I'm in third grade at Moonflower School. This school used to be a palace. But one night the whole royal family suddenly fled the palace. No one knows where they went, or why they fled!Some people think our school is haunted. Books sometimes disappear from our school. After a few days, the books return to their place. No one at our school can explain why this happens. It is said that before the royal family fled, the king's daughter used to play in the forest behind the school. Maybe she's still in the woods and comes to the school at night to wander around!

One day the school security guard said, "You kids wouldn't even be able to imagine the kind of ghosts that come to the school at night."All day long we discussed what the security guard had told us. Do ghosts really come here at night? we wondered.Hamim said, "I think they live in the forest."Antu said, "I want to see one. Should we all go to the forest tomorrow?"I was so scared. I said, "Why would we do that? I'll never go in that forest in my life."

I should not have shown how scared I was in front of everyone. From then on, Antu and Hamim always teased me about it. They wouldn't even leave me alone when I went to the bathroom. To make matters worse, I felt like the ghosts were watching me.

One day my friend Emmy brought me a gift: a beautiful walkie-talkie set. It had two small phones. When they connected, you could stand 30-50feet apart and talk to each other through them!

During lunch I took the walkie-talkies out to the field to test them out. Suddenly, Antu came and grabbed a walkie-talkie. I said, "It's a gift. Please don't take it."Antu replied, 'If you can get it back from me, you can have it."I sighed, "It would be easier to get it from the hands of ghosts than to get it back from you.""Well, go with us to the forest to see those ghosts. Then I'll give it to you," Antu said.Although I was a little scared, I agreed. I wanted to get my walkie-talkie back.Antu asked, "When will you go to the forest with us?"I said, "Let's go tomorrow. At lunchtime?"Antu responded, "Let's go tonight! It'll be fun." But nobody else agreed to go that night. So they agreed to go to the forest tomorrow at lunchtime.

That night I prepared to go to the forest. I took the slingshot out of my secret box and put it in the side pocket of my backpack. If there was any danger, I could defend myself with the slingshot.

The next day at lunchtime, we walked to the back of the school. As soon as we entered the forest, it darkened. The forest was so dense, it was as dark as night even though it was daytime. As we walked we noticed a lot of spiderwebs. Antu connected the walkie-talkies. We kept moving deeper into the forest.

A little farther ahead we saw light. The rest of the group pushed me forward. I was too scared of what they would say if I turned around, so I gathered courage and kept walking towards the light. The rest of the group stayed behind. On the walkie-talkie they said, "We're here. Keep going."

As I kept walking, different colored lights caught my eye. From what seemed like a ring of light, some colorful creatures called to me. I called Antu on the walkie-talkie. There was no response. They may have turned back.

Inside the ring I saw many creatures. They looked so innocent. Yet I still felt afraid. I slowly walked towards them.

As soon as I entered the ring, they all approached me. Getting scared, I moved backward but a group of them came up from behind me as well. I closed my eyes, afraid I was trapped in the middle of them. Suddenly, someone said, "Hello friend!" in an unfamiliar accent.I said in fear, "Who are you?""My name is Epipher. I'm reading the third grade workbook from your school. I know you. You're Onno, aren't you?" the creature replied."Yes," I said. "Are you a ghost? Is this the realm of ghosts?"

After hearing my question, Epipher seemed confused. He left to talk to someone. He came back and said, "No, no. We aren't ghosts. We come from a different galaxy. Your name is similar to our planet's name. That's why I know you so well. We are the creatures that you call 'aliens.' Creatures from a different planet."Amazed, I replied, "You're an alien! Oh my god! What's your planet called?""Bonno," Epipher told me. "It's the fifth planet in the Stenora galaxy. We're here to find new friends. But we knew nothing about humans. So I landed the spaceship in this secluded area next to the school. After you all finish school, we go in at night and secretly collect books. We also try to learn about you by hiding in the school during the day and watching you. We haven't come to harm you. We just came to see if we could be friends."I was both happy and surprised. I thought I was dreaming.

Then they gave me a tour of their spaceship. I saw someone with a book titled English for Today. He understood a little bit of the Bengali language, but he couldn't understand anything in the book because it was in English. I offered to read the book to them. They all sat around me. I read, "Cats sleep,Anywhere, any table,On top of the piano."Then I explained the poem. They excitedly grabbed my arm and asked me to bring them a cat. They had never seen such strange creatures that fall asleep anywhere!

At the end of the tour, lunchtime was also ending. We said our goodbyes for the time being. As I left I promised that I wouldn't harm them. When I got back to the school I saw Antu, Prabha, and Hamim standing there with their mouths wide open. Without saying a word, I took the walkie-talkie from Antu's hand and left for class.

After that day I was never afraid in school or in the bathroom. Occasionally I'd go to visit my friends from another planet. I'd tell them stories about our world. I'd also hear stories from them about the world of Bonno.

title: The Flying Elephant
content:
While the author, illustrator, and publisher of this book encourage and support translation of this work into other languages, they request that substantive changes to the text and art be kept to a minimum.

There once was a sugarcane farmer who lived in a small village. He worked very hard in his fields and hoped to have a big harvest.

One morning, he saw that a big chunk of his crop was missing. The next day, another huge chunk of his crop was gone. "I’ll stay awake tonight and see who’s eating my sugarcane," the farmer thought to himself.

That night, he waited by the window, watching his fields. As the moon rose, he saw a tiny speck grow larger in the sky. It was an elephant flying right into his field!

The farmer watched in amazement as it flew down and started eating his sugarcane.

He tiptoed outside and waited for the elephant to finish eating.

When the elephant began flying away, the farmer grabbed its tail. Soon he was flying above his fields into Indra’s kingdom of Paradise.

Paradise was filled with beautiful birds and flowers. The ground was covered with silver grass and precious stones.

The farmer soon found the royal palace and met Indra. "Your elephant has been flying down and eating all my sugarcane," said the farmer. "My harvest is ruined."

"I am very sorry," said Indra. "Please take whatever you want from my kingdom. I’ll make sure he doesn’t go down again and damage your crops." Indra then blessed the farmer with a safe journey home.

The farmer took two handfuls of gems and returned home.

He built himself a new house and became a very rich man. Soon the whole village was curious about his sudden wealth.

One day, some villagers went to visit the farmer’s wife. "Where did you get all this money?" they asked. "Did you find buried treasure in your fields?". The farmer’s wife told them what had happened.

That evening, the villagers decided to lure the elephant down themselves. "When we get to Paradise, we’ll take more than just two handfuls of gems!" they said.

They planted a field of sugarcane, and sure enough, the elephant flew down one night.

One villager grabbed its tail, and soon there was a chain of villagers flying behind the elephant. As they flew up, they began talking about what they would bring back from Paradise.

"I’m going to carry back this many gems!" declared the villager holding the elephant’s tail. He was so excited that he stretched his arms wide and let go of the elephant’s tail.

The villagers all fell to the ground. They watched sadly as the elephant disappeared into the sky. "Don’t worry," they said. "The elephant will come back tomorrow."

But Indra, hearing of the villagers’ trick, arranged for a sugarcane field to be planted in Paradise. The elephant never felt the need to fly down again. The villagers waited for many nights, watching the sky. But the elephant never came back down again.

title: ​Thida and the Skinny Monsters
content:
Thida grew up in a small village, far away from any city. As a child, she dreamed of becoming a doctor one day. When she was old enough, she moved to the city to attend medical school.

After many years of studying, Thida became a doctor at a regional hospital.One day, her manager at the hospital asked Thida to travel back to her home village, to help with a health problem they were having.On her way back to the village, she noticed a lot of smelly trash in the river, and flies buzzing around it.

When she arrived at the village, she saw that many people were sick, and nearly everyone was afraid."What is happening here?" Thida thought to herself.

Thida met an old friend named Sokha, who sold fruit in the village. "Many people are sick with diarrhea," Sokha said."Some people say that monsters are causing it--skinny monsters with green faces!"

Thida knew that diarrhea was a serious problem, but she also knew that it wasn’t caused by monsters."Thank you, Sokha" Thida said. "I will do my best to help.""Be careful!" Sokha said. "Don’t let the monsters get you!"

Thida knew that many things could cause a health problem like this.Before she could help, she would need to learn more.She began investigating the problem.

Thida watched a boy come out of a toilet, then pick up a piece of bread."Stop!" Thida called. "Do not eat that yet! You must wash your hands first.""Why must I wash my hands?" the boy asked. "You must clean away bacteria from the toilet that can make you sick," Thida responded.The boy agreed to wash his hands, and Thida continued her investigation.

Thida watched a girl dip her hands into a rain bucket. She raised her hands toward her mouth to drink the water."Stop!" Thida called. "Do not drink that water!" "Why not?" the girl asked."Rainwater like this often contains little creatures called parasites," Thida said. "Parasites can make you very sick. You must always boil untreated water before you drink it. That will kill the parasites, and you won’t get sick."The girl agreed to boil the water before drinking it, and Thida continued her investigation.

Thida watched a man throw an empty plastic bottle into the village lake. It was one of many pieces of trash floating in the lake. Thida had seen enough. She knew how to help the village with its health problem, and she knew that skinny monsters with green faces weren’t causing it.

Thida met with the village chief at the spirit guardian shrine in the clearing near the lake."We can fix the health problems here," she said to the chief. "But first we must understand what is causing them. Bacteria and parasites are tiny organisms that make people sick. They are to blame, not monsters.We can fight bacteria and parasites by changing our habits."

The village chief was a wise man.He brought the villagers together to learn more. Thida taught them that bacteria and parasites like dirty places, like toilets, buckets of rainwater, and lakes filled with trash.

The villagers listened carefully.They were happy to learn that a few simple changes could make their village healthy again.From that day on, they always washed their hands after using the toilet.They always boiled untreated water before drinking it.And they removed the trash from the village lake.

The people of the village stopped telling stories of skinny monsters with green faces.Now, they tell stories about Thida, the doctor who helped them be a healthy village again.

Now, whenever children see someone drop a piece of trash on the ground, they shout, "Doctor Thida told us to throw our trash in the bin!"

title: The Archer
content:
Once there was a girl from Chin State in Myanmar. Her name was Aung Ngeain, and she loved to play sports. Her favorite sport was archery, the sport of shooting arrows from a bow at a target. With the bow and arrow in her hands, Aung Ngeain felt strong.

When Aung Ngeain was 17 years old, she moved to Yangon to train with the Myanmar Archery Federation. She worked hard and learned a lot. She learned to slow down and focus on one step at a time: draw the bow, aim at the target, and release the arrow. She tested many different bows until she found the perfect fit—the compound bow, with its many wheels and pulleys.

Two years later, Aung Ngeain began to compete internationally. This was a big deal—Aung Ngeain was from a small village in Myanmar. Now she was representing her country to the whole world. But Aung Ngeain did not win right away. She grew frustrated. At times, she wanted to quit.

Her family and trainers encouraged her not to give up. So Aung Ngeain kept going to the archery range. She practiced five hours every day.

Four years later, Aung Ngeain’s hard work finally paid off. She won her first gold medal at the Asia Grand Prix 2008! And she didn't stop there. By the time she turned 28 years old, Aung Ngeain had won dozens of international medals. In 2013, she won the President’s State Excellence award for sport. Aung Ngeain did not start out as a champion. She lost many times. But with hard work and a lot of patience, she became one of the best archers in Myanmar and the world.

Use these prompts to write your own story on a piece of paper. What makes you happiest? What do you love doing? Life can be tough sometimes. Describe a tough moment in your life that you overcame. Tell a story of your future. What do you dream of doing?

Draw your portrait.

title: Please Grow
content:
What was wrong with my plants? The stem was skinny, and some leaves were turning yellow. Were my plants infected? “Sumi, please deliver these clothes,” Mom said. My plants would have to wait.

Ouch, the sun was stinging my skin. I needed to hurry. There were three addresses that I needed to deliver clothes to.

Hooray! There was only one destination left, Mbak Kinan. I’d never been to her house. Usually, Dad or Mom delivered clothes there.*Mbak is a term of respect that means “Miss” or “elder sister.” It is used in Indonesia.

I sped up so I could quickly go back to my plants. Oh no, a wheel from my basket fell off. As I was tightening the wheel, I noticed a kid biking from the corner of my eye. What was that kid doing?

“Next time be careful. Look, you ruined this plant,” I scolded him. Luckily, there were some stems that survived. Wait, this wildflower was flowering without any care. Why couldn’t my plants do the same?

I continued my walk to Mbak Kinan’s house. Ah, there was Mbak Kinan. I gave her a the bag full of clean clothes and turned to leave.

“Wait, Sumi. Please take these dirty clothes with you,” said Mbak Kinan. As I waited I noticed a plant on the railing. Where did it come from? “There are more upstairs. Do you want to see?” asked Mbak Kinan.

I definitely wanted to. I was curious what kind of plants were up there.

“Whoa! Why do you have so many vegetables, Mbak?” “To sell them. I’m farming while also attending college,” answered Mbak Kinan. Farming? How did it work?

Mbak Kinan told me about all the steps from planting the seeds to harvesting them. Turns out Mbak Kinan didn’t do it alone. Her friends helped her.

While walking around, I observed the leaves and the stems of the plants. Ah, if only my plants were this healthy.

“Mbak, I’d also like to farm, but my plants are never this fertile. Please teach me,” I said to Mbak Kinan. “That’s great, let’s start with planting the seeds,” said Mbak Kinan.

“Loosen the soil, add the compost, then mix well. Plant the seed in the soil, water it daily. After the bud has grown, move it to a bigger pot,” Mbak Kinan instructed.As I followed along, I realized the soil that I had used at home wasn’t loose enough.

“Here are some spinach seeds and fertilizer. Try to plant them at home,” said Mbak Kinan. Wow, it was my lucky day! I thanked Mbak Kinan and hurried home.

As soon as I got home, I jumped right in. Oh, I needed another pot. Aha! These used detergent containers could work as pots.

I made sure every container was clean with no soap residue. After that, I planted the seeds following Mbak Kinan’s instructions.

Done! I would wait for the spinach seeds to grow. I hoped this would work. Oh, no!

This was so troublesome. I had to start over again. I planted the remaining seeds. But what if the cats bumped into the pot again?

Aha! This place looked safe. Hopefully the thorns from the roses would protect my soon-to-be spinach.

Every day I checked on my seeds. I also remembered to water them daily.

After a week, no buds appeared. When I touched the soil, it felt dry. The sun was so hot it was drying out the soil. I knew a way to keep the soil damp! I learned it from a farming video. I waited again…

Whoa! My spinach seeds grew! Waiting for the seeds to grow had required patience. As soon as the buds appeared, I felt so happy. I smiled all day.

Day by day, the tiny buds grew bigger and bigger. The fresh leaves were ready to be harvested and enjoyed. When I grow up, I will be a farmer!

title: Dividing the Mango
content:
Meena is a little a girl who lives in a village with her parents, her grandmother, her brother Raju, and her baby sister Rani. Mithu, the parrot, is her best friend.In many ways, Meena is like any other little girl you know, but, in some ways, she is completely different.Join in Meena’s adventure as she laughs, climbs trees, asks questions,solves problems and shows you all the things a little girl can do.

One day, Meena and Mithu climbed a tall mango tree to pluck a ripe fruit. Meena ran home to share the juicy mango with her brother Raju.

Mother cut the mango and divided the pieces between Meena and Raju. Meena was upset when she saw that Raju received a bigger share of the mango. When she protested, her grandmother said that boys always get more to eat than girls.

That night, too, Meena noticed that Raju was given more food than she was. Mother also gave him an egg, while Meena got none. Mithu watched from behind and was not at all pleased.

When the children went to wash their hands, Mithu divided the egg into two and put half of it on Meena’s plate.

When they came back, Mother told Meena to give the egg back to Raju.

Grandmother started scolding Meena for wanting the egg, but Father thought it was unfair because both children were growing up, and they both worked hard.

Raju didn’t agree. He thought he worked very hard, much harder than Meena, and therefore deserved more food. "Your work is so simple," he told her. So Meena suggested that they change places for a day and do each other’s chores. Raju agreed.

The next day was a holiday. Meena asked Mithu to wake Raju up early in the morning to light the fire.

Raju discovered that lighting the fire was not an easy job.

Next, he had to sweep the yard …

…and then feed the hungry chickens, who jumped all over him.

Meena took Lali, the cow, out to graze.

While Raju collected the cow dung, scrubbed the dishes …

…washed the clothes …

…and filled the pots with water, Meena sat dozing under a tree.

Suddenly, Mithu woke her up screaming, "Lali! Lali!"

Meena found out that Lali had wandered into the headman’s vegetable garden. She had to chase Lali for a long time before she was able to catch her.

Meena finally returned home. Raju was looking after baby Rani.

Raju was tired and hungry. Grandmother had watched him all day and had realized just how much work Meena did every day.

That night at dinner, Mother gave Raju Meena’s usual share of food, and put the larger plate of food in front of Meena.

Poor Raju looked so disappointed! Looking at his face, everyone burst out laughing. Everyone now knew that boys and girls need equal food to grow strong.

On the way to school the next morning, Raju plucked a ripe guava that was hanging from a low branch.

As he shared the fruit with Meena, Raju promised to help her with the housework whenever he could. Meena admitted that Raju’s work of looking after Lali was not very easy, either.

The Meena Communication Initiative was launched by UNICEF in the 19 90 sin an effort to impart important messages on gender, child rights, education, protection and development and to inspire girls, their families and communities across South Asia through animated films, comic books and radio series, among other products.

title: Nawawala si Pluto
content:
The sun looked far out into space. "Is one of my planets missing?"She asked the planets to line up, then put on her glasses and counted. "Oh no!" she cried. "Where did little Pluto go?"

She reached out to Mercury with one of her rays. "Have you seen Pluto anywhere?" Mercury scratched his craters.

"Little blue Pluto? I haven't seen him, where did he go?" Mercury replied.

So Mercury went to Venus and asked, "Have you seen Pluto anywhere?"

"How should I know where frozen little Pluto has gone?" Venus answered, as a few of her volcanoes erupted.

So Mercury and Venus went to Earth and asked, "Have you seen Pluto anywhere?"

The ocean waves rose anxiously over Earth. "Pluto with the unusual orbit?" she asked. "I can't say I've seen him."

So Mercury, Venus, and Earth went to Mars and asked, "Have you seen Pluto anywhere?"

Mars turned really red, then answered sheepishly, "Pluto lives in the Kuiper belt doesn't he? I haven't seen him there lately."

So, Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars went to Jupiter and asked, "Have you seen Pluto anywhere?"

Jupiter rotated quickly, looking everywhere for Pluto. "Pluto's rotation is so slow, I haven't seen him in quite a while."

So Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter went to Saturn and asked, "Have you seen Pluto anywhere?"

Saturn spun around inside her rings before answering, "Oh, poor Pluto with the weakest gravity of all. I have not seen him anywhere."

So Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn went to Uranus and asked, "Have you seen Pluto anywhere?"

Uranus, who really wanted to go to bed, stretched and yawned, then finally said, "No, but I wish he was around, so I could count his five moons to help me get to sleep."

So Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, and Uranus went to Neptune who was shivering cold and asked, "Have you seen Pluto anywhere? He's your closest neighbor. Surely you would know where he has gone!

Neptune shook off some snow, then said, "I saw him pack his bags. He seemed so gloomy and sad. But he would not tell me where he was going or why."

Suddenly, the planets heard someone crying nearby. They all hurried to see what was going on.

Pluto was sitting alone, out of his orbit, crying. The planets were so happy to finally find Pluto! They asked him why he disappeared. "The scientists banned me from being a planet because I am small and I can’t clear large objects from my orbit."

Just then, Sun arrived. "That doesn’t matter," she said with a warmth that reached all the way to Pluto's chilly heart. "You’ll always be part of our family, the solar system family!"

The planets all cheered with glee, "We are a family! The solar system family!"

THE END

title: Rain
content:
I love water.

I enjoy playing with water.

It is raining.

Rain gives us water.

I enjoy playing outside.

But it is raining.

I enjoy playing out in the rain.

My hair is wet from playing in the rain. My father is fixing my hair.

title: Day and Night
content:
Long ago, the sun was very lazy. it shined whenever it wanted to.

The rooster crowed cock-a-doodle-doo, but the sun didn’t come out.

The sun wouldn’t shine. The star and the moon had to work hard without getting any rest.

They went to see the sun to divide time amongst them, but the sun wouldn’t follow.

The moon and the star thus asked for help from the sky.

The sky decided for them to divide time into day and night.

If the sun would not do as said, then the sun would not be allowed into the sky.

The rooster crowed when the sun rose in the morning and when the sun set in the evening.

The moon and stars shined at night.

From then on, the sun worked diligently and shined in the day.

The sun, the moon, and the stars happily shined at the right time.

title: The Kingdom of Change
content:
One hundred years ago, there was a kingdom called Carimbala. This kingdom was ruled by King Mauleto. The people in Carimbala never spoke up about problems because King Mauleto ruled in a very tough way.

“Daddy, I want to become a teacher!” Kaisose told her father, Agosto. Agosto answered, “Who do you want to teach? The soldiers? You’re not brave enough to teach. Look—there are no women teachers.”

Kaisose felt sad to hear this. Schools for little girls who wanted to be teachers did not exist in Carimbala.

One morning, the sun shone beautifully on the kingdom of Carimbala. People were preparing to welcome King Manduki and King Fatukboot from the two great kingdoms that surrounded Carimbala.

With a friendly, smiling face, King Mauleto welcomed his guests.

The ceremony began, and King Manduki said to King Mauleto, “This kingdom is so united. I heard that you built a new school here?” “Yes, sir,” King Mauleto replied.

Suddenly a little voice said, “But we cannot go to the school!” That voice came from Kaisose, who was standing in a tall tree.

Kaisose’s father and mother were shocked and scared.

Then Kaisose yelled, “The king does not allow us to go to the school. I cannot become a teacher. Girls just stay at home and do things like cook and get water. We are not happy.”

King Mauleto was embarrassed. He had not expected this to happen.

King Manduki and King Fatukboot were angry that King Mauleto had lied about how happy his people were. Mauleto was forced to give up his crown.

While waiting for King Mauleto’s replacement to be named, Kaisose was entrusted with taking care of Carimbala and communicating with King Manduki’s and King Fatukboot’s kingdoms. Thanks to Kaisose’s courage, all women were able to go to school.

Children need books with characters, themes, and settings that reflect and affirm their lives and provide opportunities to explore the world.

title: Sister! Sister! Where Does Thunder Come From?
content:
Sister, sister I wonder... What do you wonder, little brother, What do you wonder? I wonder, I wonder, Where thunder comes from. Where do you think, little brother, Where do you think? I think, I think Tell me, little brother, What do you think?

I think That there is a great big Kumbhakarna Sleeping in the sky And when the silver ropes of rain Lash him, and chase his sleep away, He wakes up. Sparks fly out of his eyes like lightning He stamps his big ugly feet Takes a long deep breath And ROARS with rage.

(Let me tell you If I had thrown a tantrum like that Mother would have spanked me. Hard.) I think that's Where the thunder comes from From the fury of a Kumbhakarna in the sky Who likes to stay asleep, and dry. I am clever, aren't I, sister?

Oh yes you are, little brother, oh yes you are. And maybe you're right, too... But in the books that I have read That is not what they said. Then what did they say, sister, What did they say? What do you think, little brother, What do you think? I think, I think... Tell me, little brother, What do you think?

I think There is a gang of crazy bikers Up there in the sky In their black leather jackets And steel-studded boots And dark glasses that hide their eyes Just like in the movies. And what they like to do best Is to race each other in the pouring rain.

I think When they mount their bikes and KICK them to life Steel strikes steel There's your lightning! Then, when they do what bikers do Rev up their engines, and rrrev them, and rrrev them There's your thunder!

I think that's where the thunder comes from Not from a demon, not from a plane, But from a fleet of bikes that race in the rain. I'm clever, aren't I, sister?

I know you are, little brother, I know you are And maybe you're right, too. But in all the books that I have read That is not what they said. Then what did they say, sister, What did they say? What do you think, little brother, What do you think? I think, I think... Tell me, little brother, What do you think?

I think That when it rains The children Of the old woman in the sky Are absolutely NOT allowed To play outside (for they may catch a cold!). Cooped up indoors They all get a little restless, and VERY cranky.

I think the old woman opens her trunk Pulls out a game of chaupad And a pair of giant dice. The children clap their hands in excitement Roll the giant dice And forget they were ever bored. I think that's where the thunder comes from From the dance of a pair of dice As they make their way across the skies. I'm clever, aren't I, sister?

Of course you are, little brother, And maybe you're right, too... But in all the books that I have read That is not what they said. Then what did they say, sister, What did they say? Come here, little brother, I'll tell you what they said. They said, they said... Tell me sister, what did they say?

They said That thunder always comes after lightning. But you know that, don't you? And that It is the lightning That makes the thunder.

The lightning is like ELEC-TRI-CITY The same magic ELEC-TRI-CITY That runs the pump And floods the house with light And fills the TV with Sachin and Saurav At the flip of a switch. But I asked about thunder, sister, I asked about thunder. Have patience, little brother, Have patience now.

They said that lightning is very hot Just like electricity. And when it slices through the air And stabs the earth It makes the air through which it comes Very Very Very hot. They said The hot air EXPANDS And explodes BOOOOOOM! Like a monster Diwali bomb.

And some little children Bury their faces In their mothers' sarees. But brave little boys like you Hear the air go BOOOOOOM! Turn around quickly. Can it be true, sister, can it be true? I can't say, little brother, I can't say. But in all the books that I have read That is what they said.

FIND OUT MORE! Where does thunder come from? Everything around us is made up of tiny particles called atoms. Each atom has a nucleus at the centre, which is filled with particles called neutrons and positively charged particles called protons. Even tinier particles (negatively charged) called electrons go around the nucleus like the planets go around the sun. In a thundercloud, air carries bits of ice and water droplets upwards. When they rub against each other, the atoms in them become ions (that is, they become charged positively or negatively). The positive ions are lighter and move upwards, while the heavier negative ions move downwards to the bottom of the cloud.

The negative ions at the bottom of the cloud attract the positive ions on the earth. When they start flowing towards each other, electricity is created, which becomes a huge, powerful flash of lightning. The lightning makes the air around it very, very hot almost as hot as the sun! This hot air expands very quickly, causing a big explosion. It then begins to contract equally quickly once the lightning flash has passed. This explosion of air is what causes the sound waves that we call thunder.

Try this experiment! To understand how particles with opposite charges attract each other, let's make a magic magnetic balloon! You need: A balloon A piece of wool or silk A wall What to do: 1. Blow up the balloon. 2. Rub it briskly with the piece of wool or silk. 3. Hold it against the wall and watch it stick there like a magnet to iron! Why does this happen? When you rub the balloon with the wool or silk, electrons get transferred between the two. The atoms in the balloon take in more electrons, so the balloon becomes negatively charged. When you hold it against the wall, the negative ions in the balloon get attracted to the positive ions in the wall, causing the balloon to stick to the wall!

title: Off to an Island Reunion
content:
The ocean makes Maraia smile. She can stare at it all day long. Sometimes blue, sometimes green. But always shimmering. Best of all, Maraia can enjoy it without hearing a thing.

Bobo loves the ocean too. He is also the only one who hears and understands Maraia’s thoughts. The two friends are going to a family reunion on Maraia’s drua.

Bobo thumps his tail on the deck. He cocks his head as if to say, “Are we there yet?” “Almost there, Bobo!” Maraia points to the island.

Bobo is bounding about the deck with his tail wagging furiously. He is too excited to keep still. He places his paw on Maraia’s hand. It is his way of saying “thank you.” “You are welcome, Bobo. You are part of my family too.”

The drua speeds toward Via Island. Bobo feels that something is bothering Maraia. He licks her hand as if to say, “What’s wrong?”

“It will be good to see my family again,” thinks Maraia. She sighs loudly. “But I hope they remember that I can play their games too even though I cannot hear them.”

But no one remembers. No one remembers that Maraia can play all their games too.

No one remembers … except Lisa.“Hello, Maraia. How are you?” Cousin Lisa signs. “Look, I learned the Fijian Sign Language after our last family reunion.”

Maraia’s eyes widen and her jaw drops. She turns to Bobo and thinks, “Is she speaking to us?” “Yes, yes!” Bobo runs around them in circles with his tail wagging furiously.

But then Maraia frowns slightly. “I don’t understand you though,” she tries to tell Lisa with her hands.

Cousin Lisa smiles at Maraia. She holds her hand and moves toward a large rain tree. They find a nice shady spot and begin to talanoa. Even though they use different hand signs, they are still able to understand each other. After a while, the other cousins join them too.

Maraia’s cousins love her drua. For the rest of the week, they spend their days zipping around the lagoon.

Cousin Lisa teaches them how to sign their favorite words during these ocean romps.

Time flies as they enjoy themselves, and soon it is time to leave. Although they are sad, the cousins agree to learn the Fijian Sign Language before their next reunion. Maraia beams proudly at her cousins. She still cannot believe they are all going to learn sign language together.

Best of all, everyone comes to see Maraia and Bobo off.

Wonderful Wordsdrua – a traditional double-hulled canoe created in Fijitalanoa – to chat, or to tell a story in the Fijian language-------------------------------------------------------------Sign language is used by deaf people to communicate using gestures. These gestures include hand movements and facial expressions. There are more than 300 sign languages in the world. Different sign languages are used in different countries and regions.

title: Try Again!
content:
Look! Look!What’s on that mangrove branch?Archie and his friends get ready.Insects make delicious prey.

Hey, there’s a shrimp! Archie wants to play. Archie’s friends remind him This is hunting time. Archie does not listen.

The shrimp crawls away. It disappears among the rocks. Archie gives up going after it. He’s still hungry.

Archie looks for his friends. They have finished hunting and eating. Now he has to hunt alone. Archie is sure he can do it.

Wow, there’s a fat beetle! One, two, three … shoot! Yay! he hits it. A fat beetle is a delightful prey.

Zzzzzz! Oh No! the beetle escapes! Maybe it is too big. Archie’s shot is not strong enough.

Archie looks for another prey. There it is! One …two … three, shoot! Yes, his shot is spot on!

Archie is famished. He can’t wait to eat his catch. But … Gulp! A halfbeak fish gets to it first and gobbles it up.

Archie is starving.

What must Archie do?

Archie wants to get his prey back. But, without food, he feels too weak to fight.

Archie lets it go. He swims away from the estuary.

Oh! It’s dazzling here! The mangroves have been cut.There are no more branches for the insects. Archie cannot find prey here.

The mangrove roots are dead. Without them, the water has become murky. There is nothing to hold back the sand and mud. Archie can hardly swim.

The halfbeak fish is not behind Archie anymore. He must have had enough to eat. Archie turns back toward the estuary.

Yay! A cricket!

One …two … three, shoot! Oh no … no jet of water comes out of his mouth. Try again, try again! Archie spits and spits until he can’t do it anymore.

Archie hears blurred noises from behind. His friends have come! They offer their help.

Archie does not want to bother his friends. Anyway, it is his fault. He should not have gone after the shrimp.

Archie gathers his strength and collects enough water in his mouth. His friends cheer him on. Try again! One …two … three, shoot!

Hurray! It’s time to eat!

Next time, Archie will not stray away from his friends. When they are together, the halfbeak fish will stay away.

Archie is an archer fish. An archer fish hunts by spitting a jet of water from its mouth. They prey on insects in the mangrove forest. Mangroves are plants that grow in brackish waters (a mix of salt and fresh water).Mangrove forests are important because they help to protect coastal areas from tidal waves and erosion. The mangrove fruit is a favourite food for storks, water lizards, and monkeys.

title: The Dry Season Concert
content:
It's hot today, though a cool breeze blows in the cicadas' garden.The dry season is almost here.It's time for the cicadas to hold a welcoming concert.Pangpung, the concert conductor, must make sure everything goes well.This concert has to be perfect, and it has to be on time.

"Attention cicadas! We will rehearse this afternoon. Please be there!" Pangpung shouts, and flies around."Remember this! Never sing too loud in rehearsal, okay?"

Their first rehearsal begins."Psstt! Please lower your voice! This is just a rehearsal, not the concert itself!" Pangpung screams.

The next day, the sky is filled with clouds.Pangpung doubts the rehearsal can be held that afternoon."Ah, perhaps the clouds will be gone later," Pangpung thinks.

That afternoon, the cicadas continue with the rehearsal.But then, suddenly, rain starts to pour from the sky.

The heavy wind blows Pangpung and his friends."All, find shelter! Hold on tight!" Pangpung screams loudly.The cicadas think the weather is so confusing!

The next day, the weather is finally clear, and the cicadas begin their rehearsal. As always, Pangpung reminds his friends, "The concert has to be performed on time!"

"Don’t be too loud. This is just a rehearsal!""Dry season is not here yet. There aren't many fallen leaves from the rosewood tree.""Don't be too loud! The kapok tree flowers haven't yet bloomed."Oh, Pangpung never gets tired of reminding his friends.

Some of the cicadas feel that Pangpung is too bossy, and they don't want to be in the concert anymore."It's okay," Pangpung thinks.He can still lead his other friends.

That day, Pangpung sees that the leaves from the rosewood tree have started to fall."Oh, wow…Dry season will be here soon!"

Now even the kapok tree flowers have bloomed!"Yay! Dry season is really here. It's already here!" Pangpung tells his friends.They have to organize the concert to welcome the dry season…IMMEDIATELY!This has to be a perfect concert. And after the concert, all the cicadas plan to dance on the stage together.

In the morning, all the cicadas perform in their last rehearsal.They practice hard and sing a very beautiful song.At noon tomorrow, the Dry Season Concert will be performed just in time.

The concert stage has already been built.All the insects have accepted the invitation to the concert.Everything is perfect.Now it's time for Pangpung to get some sleep before his big day tomorrow.

The day has come.The sky is clear, and the weather is warm. All the insects have come from all over the garden.They talk to one another about the upcoming dry season.

It's time for Pangpung to conduct the concert.Finally, the Dry Season Concert begins.The shrilling voices of the cicadas melodiously flow all over the garden."Screech, screech, screech…!""Screech, screech, screech…!"

But suddenly…waterdrops fall down all over the cicadas.What should they do?

"Why is there rain?" Pangpung yells.The cicada voices become softer and softer as time goes by.Meanwhile, the audience is running around, trying to find shelter.

However, Pangpung insists on conducting the concert."Hey, the rain is not that heavy anymore!" He urges his friends to continue singing. "Let's keep our spirits up!" Pangpung leads his friends again and again as a good conductor does.

The cicadas sing their song again with their shrill and melodious voices. Then the confusing rainstorm stops, and the sun shines beautifully.They close the concert with a happy dance.

title: All By Myself
content:
I'm a big sister now. Mom says I can take the bus to school all by myself!

There's my bus."Wait for me!" I call.

"Good morning, everyone."

I look out the window as we go.There's a building with large square panels.

It's the aquarium.The aquarium is on the way to school.

On another street, I see a giant statue in front of a palace.

I imagine the giant statue chasing me.Eeek!

The bus goes under an overpass.

Then it goes down a busy street.

I know this shop! There's the cat that sells donuts.

And there's the kite shop.School is not far away.

Finally, we reach my school.

I rode the bus to school all by myself!
